PMFBYGrievance-v0.1.name: PMFBYGrievance
PMFBYGrievance-v0.1.description: Attributes for grievances raised against the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana crop insurance scheme. This is an API schema, not a domain schema: it describes what the PMFBY grievance API accepts and returns, so an experience layer can call it without reading adapter mapping files. Attaches through commitmentAttributes: a grievance is a promise with a lifecycle of its own, not a catalogable resource. Extends GrievanceBase, in api-schemas/Grievance/v0.1. The base owns the field set every grievance pack shares and the vocabulary those fields are written in; this file pins @type and scheme to PMFBY, adds what PMFBY alone has -- the phone, the application, the season, the OTP challenge and the ticket number -- and records against each inherited field how this portal fills it. Nothing grievance-related is added to a domain schema: a grievance is a Provider's API surface, not a thing the network describes. Direction is carried by informationMode, never by the Beckn action. OnDemand is the ask, Direct is an answer carrying a real case. The same attributes serve init and status without change. On support the payload attaches through channels instead, and three fields move into the Support object itself. The channel also carries provider, which exists for that action alone: a SupportAction composes no Contract, so the adapter has nowhere else to read the provider from. The grievance is lodged with support, not confirm, so no confirm entry appears below. x-beckn-container-by-action says which container each action uses, and the per-field x-beckn-path says where a field that moves ends up.

pack_fields.description: Canonical OAN type, optionally accompanied by Provider-defined JSON-LD types.

Mobile number of the farmer raising the grievance, and the number the portal sends the OTP to. Ten digits, Indian mobile series. Never returned in a response; on_init carries the masked challengeIssued.sentTo instead.

PMFBY crop insurance application number the grievance concerns. On support it is the orderId, the thing support is required against, and it holds that meaning in both directions: the ask sends it and on_support echoes it unchanged. The ticket the portal issues does not go there -- it comes back in ticketNo on the channel, because a ticket is not what the complaint is against.

Crop year of the application, as a four-digit year. The portal returns request_year as a number, so the adapter stringifies it on the way back. It is the year of the application, not of the grievance: a 2025 crop year can carry a 2026 complaint date.

Crop season of the application. PMFBY accepts three seasons and nothing else. The network carries the name; the adapter maps it to the numeric request_season the portal wants -- Kharif 1, Rabi 2, Zaid 3. Summer is the same season as Zaid and is sent as Zaid.

Category of the grievance. The code is the portal's category and sub-category joined by a dot, and the adapter splits it on that dot into two upstream fields, so the shape is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. The portal returns a name for each half on a case read and the adapter joins them with a slash, so name follows code. The portal publishes no list of valid pairs; see the pack README.

pack_fields.requirement: At least one of code or name
pack_fields.description: Category and sub-category joined by a dot, exactly as the portal numbers them.

Proof of the phone number, presented when filing. No correlator field exists, and additionalProperties refuses one: PMFBY binds the challenge to the phone number alone and issues none, so a caller sending one is confused about the mechanism rather than being quietly ignored.
writeOnly is the contract: the whole object travels inbound only. It must never be returned in any response, written to a log, or attached to a trace, and the value is never forwarded to the lodge call.

Authentication mechanism. PMFBY offers one: a six-digit OTP texted to the registered mobile number. Supporting a second mechanism later is widening this enum and pinning the format its value takes; nothing about the carrier changes.

The OTP itself, six digits, since the portal rejects any other length. The pattern is what enforces that -- allOf narrowing is evaluated, so the rule is held by the pack and not left to a mapping guard.
writeOnly is the contract: it travels inbound only and must never be returned in a response, written to a log, or attached to a trace.

Portal grievance ticket number. Returned when a grievance is filed and presented again to read its replies, so it travels in both directions. It stays in the attributes on every leg -- no x-beckn-path moves it -- so on_support returns it here and leaves orderId holding the application number it arrived with. Digits only, and long enough not to be mistaken for a phone number: the live system routes a ten-digit answer to the phone and anything longer to the ticket, and observed tickets run twelve to fifteen digits. The exact length is not pinned because that range is described as typical, not as a rule; the maxLength is a sanity bound well clear of it, not a statement about the format.

Acknowledgement that the portal has sent a challenge. Carries no secret: the OTP itself is never returned. No correlator field exists and additionalProperties refuses one, since PMFBY issues none. readOnly is the contract: this is returned and never sent.
Mechanism the portal used. PMFBY offers SMS_OTP only.

Masked destination, so the farmer can confirm which number was used without the number being disclosed. PMFBY sends to a phone, so the mask is a phone mask -- first two and last two digits only, the six between them always X.
When the challenge stops being accepted. Required because the adapter always derives one, so a caller may rely on it.
Pinned to PMFBY: this pack describes one scheme and nothing else, so there is exactly one legal value for code. The title in the examples is "Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana".
The scheme this pack describes.

PMFBY note: name carries the portal's TicketStatus phrase. The portal also returns a numeric TicketStatusID, an opaque internal key that is not mapped -- the derived code replaces it. A lodge reply carries no status at all, so there is nothing to quote and code stands alone.
PMFBY note: read from ComplaintDate, which the portal already sends as ISO. On a lodge the adapter generates it.

PMFBY note: read from latestRemark. The portal sends an empty string while no remark exists; the adapter omits the field rather than passing the empty string through. PMFBY publishes no companion date, which is why this pack refuses remarkedOn.

fields.description:
Direction of this payload. OnDemand is the ask; Direct is an answer carrying a real case.
Direction is carried by this field and never by the Beckn action, so the same attributes serve every leg without change.

The portal this grievance belongs to: who it is filed with on the way in, and who the case came from on the way out. One field for both, because on a grievance they are always the same party -- the adapter reads a case back from the portal it filed with, and no third party stands between them.
Carried in the attributes on the support leg only, and only because a SupportAction composes no Contract: every other action has one, and there the same fact is read from commitments[].offer.provider.
Same shape in both places, deliberately. A reader writes .provider.id on support and .provider.id on the contract, and the adapter's own binding path says channels[].provider.id against a Beckn v2 default of commitments[].offer.provider.id -- the same grammar, the same tail, a different container.
scheme.code names a scheme rather than a participant, so it cannot stand in.
Not required, and deliberately not part of a Direct guard. On a contract leg the attributes genuinely do not carry it -- Beckn's offer does -- so requiring it here would force a second copy into commitmentAttributes.
Network participant id, lower-case, matching the registry exactly. This is the only field the adapter routes on.
How the portal is named to a reader. Only name is required; the routing is done on id.

Human-readable name of the provider. Beckn requires a Provider to carry a descriptor, and a name is the only part of one worth carrying here -- a code would merely repeat id.
Advisory, and never authoritative: the registry owns this word. The adapter reads id and ignores name, so a caller that sends a stale name is routed correctly anyway. It is required because a participant id alone makes a payload unreadable to anyone without the registry open.
Pinned to PMFBY: this pack describes one scheme and nothing else, so there is exactly one legal value for code. The title in the examples is "Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana".
The scheme this pack describes.

The farmer's account of the problem, in their own words. A minimum length because a grievance that says nothing cannot be acted on, and a maximum because this is unvalidated free text arriving from a caller and going on to the portal. Neither portal publishes an upper limit, so the bound is the network's own and matches caseRemark: 2000 characters, long enough for any real account of a problem.
Does not travel inside the attributes object. x-beckn-path moves it to the Beckn descriptor, which is where a contract says what it is about -- so a client that does not know the pack still sees what was complained about.
fields.example: "Claim approved in July but no amount has been credited to my account."

fields.description:
Where the grievance stands. code is the network's CaseStatusCode, which is what a client branches on; name is the portal's own status phrase, kept verbatim, which is what the farmer is shown.
code is required and name is not, and the absence of name is informative: it is how a client tells a state the adapter inferred from one the portal stated.
A phrase the adapter does not recognise maps to UnderReview, keeping the phrase in name -- never to a terminal state, which must come from the portal. The adapter may infer a state; it must never infer that a case is finished.
The enum is not narrowed in either pack. Neither portal publishes a full status vocabulary, so narrowing would be a guess that rejects a legitimate state.

PMFBY note: name carries the portal's TicketStatus phrase. The portal also returns a numeric TicketStatusID, an opaque internal key that is not mapped -- the derived code replaces it. A lodge reply carries no status at all, so there is nothing to quote and code stands alone.

Where a case stands, in the network's own vocabulary, rather than in the portal's wording.
The split is deliberate. code is the network's word and is what a client branches on; the accompanying descriptor name is the portal's own phrase, kept verbatim, and is what a farmer is shown. A portal phrase the adapter does not recognise maps to UnderReview -- non-terminal, and honest -- with the phrase preserved in name. The adapter may infer a state; it must never infer that a case is finished, so anything unmapped stays non-terminal.
One list, shared by every grievance pack. A portal vocabulary is not enumerated anywhere: portals add phrases without notice, and the mapping from phrase to code is the adapter's job.
fields.constraints: enum: Registered, UnderReview, AwaitingApplicant, Replied, Resolved, Rejected, Closed

enum_details.meaning: Lodged and acknowledged by the portal, not yet picked up.
Being worked by the portal. Also the fallback for a portal phrase the adapter does not recognise.
Blocked on the applicant -- a document or a clarification is needed before work can continue.
A response has been recorded against the case, which remains open.

Closed without action; the case was refused.
Closed with no further action -- lapsed, withdrawn, or closed automatically.

Date the grievance was filed with the portal. An IST calendar date: an adapter must take today's date in IST and not from a UTC clock, which would record the previous day for anything filed before 05:30 IST.

Named for the case rather than for an author: a remark may come from a reviewing officer, from a body handling the claim, or from the system closing a record, and neither portal publishes a reliable author. Absent rather than empty while nothing has been recorded, so an absent field reads as "nothing recorded yet". Bounded at 2000 characters because it is unvalidated upstream free text being placed in a response.

PMKISANGrievance-v0.1.name: PMKISANGrievance
PMKISANGrievance-v0.1.description: Attributes for grievances raised against the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi income-support scheme. This is an API schema, not a domain schema: it describes what the PM-KISAN grievance API accepts and returns, so an experience layer can call it without reading adapter mapping files. Attaches through commitmentAttributes: a grievance is a promise with a lifecycle of its own, not a catalogable resource. Extends GrievanceBase, in api-schemas/Grievance/v0.1. The base owns the field set every grievance pack shares and the vocabulary those fields are written in; this file pins @type and scheme to PM-KISAN, adds the one field PM-KISAN alone has -- the registration number -- declares its own closed category vocabulary, and records against each inherited field how this portal fills it. Nothing grievance-related is added to a domain schema: a grievance is a Provider's API surface, not a thing the network describes. Direction is carried by informationMode, never by the Beckn action. OnDemand is the ask, Direct is an answer carrying a real case. There is no init leg: PM-KISAN issues no challenge, so the payload rides on channels for support and on commitmentAttributes for status, and nothing else. x-beckn-container-by-action says which container each action uses, and the per-field x-beckn-path says where a field that moves ends up.

pack_fields.description: Canonical OAN type, optionally accompanied by Provider-defined JSON-LD types.

The PM-KISAN registration number the grievance is filed under. It is both the identity the portal authenticates on and the enrolment the complaint is against, because PM-KISAN has no separate reference for either -- the upstream takes one field, IdentityNo, and nothing else names a case. That is why it carries the same x-beckn-path as PMFBY's applicationNo: on support it is the orderId, the thing support is required against.
Named for the enrolment rather than for the applicant. An earlier draft called it applicantId, which claimed the field names a person and sat one letter from PMFBY's applicantPhone -- inviting a caller to read the two as the same role and put a phone number in orderId. It names neither a person nor a contact: it names the enrolment a complaint is filed against, which is what applicationNo names on PMFBY. The two ends match so the pair reads as one slot.
Aadhaar is deliberately not accepted. The portal takes a token derived from one through /GrievanceAadhaarToken and carries it in the same IdentityNo field, which would make this value sometimes a stable reference and sometimes an ephemeral secret. Registration numbers only keeps it one thing, and keeps the upstream Type field a constant.
Not writeOnly, and no-echo is deliberately absent: the value is returned in orderId, which is the provider's slot to fill. Sending back the caller's own registration number over the same signed exchange it arrived on discloses nothing. no-log and no-trace are the markings that matter here and they are unconditional.
The rule is only non-empty and alphanumeric. Eleven alphanumeric characters is the documented shape, but nothing upstream enforces it, and a length rule taken from a tool docstring would reject a valid grievance before the farmer's complaint reached the portal. ASCII-only is on purpose: the upstream accepts Devanagari and other native-script digits and forwards them unconverted.

Category of the grievance. Unlike PMFBY, the portal publishes a closed list of ten codes, so the pack enumerates them and an unknown code is refused at the network edge rather than upstream. The code goes to the portal verbatim.

pack_fields.requirement: At least one of code or name

fields.description:
Direction of this payload. OnDemand is the ask; Direct is an answer carrying a real case.
Direction is carried by this field and never by the Beckn action, so the same attributes serve every leg without change.

The portal this grievance belongs to: who it is filed with on the way in, and who the case came from on the way out. One field for both, because on a grievance they are always the same party -- the adapter reads a case back from the portal it filed with, and no third party stands between them.
Carried in the attributes on the support leg only, and only because a SupportAction composes no Contract: every other action has one, and there the same fact is read from commitments[].offer.provider.
Same shape in both places, deliberately. A reader writes .provider.id on support and .provider.id on the contract, and the adapter's own binding path says channels[].provider.id against a Beckn v2 default of commitments[].offer.provider.id -- the same grammar, the same tail, a different container.
scheme.code names a scheme rather than a participant, so it cannot stand in.
Not required, and deliberately not part of a Direct guard. On a contract leg the attributes genuinely do not carry it -- Beckn's offer does -- so requiring it here would force a second copy into commitmentAttributes.
Network participant id, lower-case, matching the registry exactly. This is the only field the adapter routes on.
How the portal is named to a reader. Only name is required; the routing is done on id.

Human-readable name of the provider. Beckn requires a Provider to carry a descriptor, and a name is the only part of one worth carrying here -- a code would merely repeat id.
Advisory, and never authoritative: the registry owns this word. The adapter reads id and ignores name, so a caller that sends a stale name is routed correctly anyway. It is required because a participant id alone makes a payload unreadable to anyone without the registry open.
Pinned to PM-KISAN: this pack describes one scheme and nothing else, so there is exactly one legal value for code. The title in the examples is "Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi".
The scheme this pack describes.

The farmer's account of the problem, in their own words. A minimum length because a grievance that says nothing cannot be acted on, and a maximum because this is unvalidated free text arriving from a caller and going on to the portal. Neither portal publishes an upper limit, so the bound is the network's own and matches caseRemark: 2000 characters, long enough for any real account of a problem.
Does not travel inside the attributes object. x-beckn-path moves it to the Beckn descriptor, which is where a contract says what it is about -- so a client that does not know the pack still sees what was complained about.

PM-KISAN note: the inherited minimum length is measured on the raw string, while the upstream client measures it after trimming -- so ten characters of whitespace pass here and fail there. The adapter trims before sending and re-checks.
fields.example: "Third instalment for 2026 has not been credited."

fields.description:
Where the grievance stands. code is the network's CaseStatusCode, which is what a client branches on; name is the portal's own status phrase, kept verbatim, which is what the farmer is shown.
code is required and name is not, and the absence of name is informative: it is how a client tells a state the adapter inferred from one the portal stated.
A phrase the adapter does not recognise maps to UnderReview, keeping the phrase in name -- never to a terminal state, which must come from the portal. The adapter may infer a state; it must never infer that a case is finished.
The enum is not narrowed in either pack. Neither portal publishes a full status vocabulary, so narrowing would be a guess that rejects a legitimate state.

PM-KISAN note: name carries the portal's GrievanceStatus phrase. Where GrievanceStatus is missing the adapter infers Replied or UnderReview according to whether a remark is present, and a lodge reply carries no status of any kind, so Registered is asserted. In all three cases code stands alone.

Where a case stands, in the network's own vocabulary, rather than in the portal's wording.
The split is deliberate. code is the network's word and is what a client branches on; the accompanying descriptor name is the portal's own phrase, kept verbatim, and is what a farmer is shown. A portal phrase the adapter does not recognise maps to UnderReview -- non-terminal, and honest -- with the phrase preserved in name. The adapter may infer a state; it must never infer that a case is finished, so anything unmapped stays non-terminal.
One list, shared by every grievance pack. A portal vocabulary is not enumerated anywhere: portals add phrases without notice, and the mapping from phrase to code is the adapter's job.
fields.constraints: enum: Registered, UnderReview, AwaitingApplicant, Replied, Resolved, Rejected, Closed

enum_details.meaning: Lodged and acknowledged by the portal, not yet picked up.
Being worked by the portal. Also the fallback for a portal phrase the adapter does not recognise.
Blocked on the applicant -- a document or a clarification is needed before work can continue.
A response has been recorded against the case, which remains open.
Closed with action taken.
Closed without action; the case was refused.
Closed with no further action -- lapsed, withdrawn, or closed automatically.

fields.description:
Date the grievance was filed with the portal. An IST calendar date: an adapter must take today's date in IST and not from a UTC clock, which would record the previous day for anything filed before 05:30 IST.

PM-KISAN note: read from the portal on a case read; generated by the adapter on a lodge, because the lodge reply carries no date. It is also half the case selector -- see the guard below.

The most recent remark recorded against the case. Named for the case rather than for an author: a remark may come from a reviewing officer, from a body handling the claim, or from the system closing a record, and neither portal publishes a reliable author. It is an annotation on a record, not necessarily a reply addressed to the farmer.
Absent rather than empty while nothing has been recorded, so an absent field reads as "nothing recorded yet". Bounded at 2000 characters because it is unvalidated upstream free text being placed in a response.

PM-KISAN note: read from OfficerReply. Its companion date is OfficeReplyDate -- an office rather than an officer, which is one reason the network does not adopt the portal's field name.
fields.example: "Bank account seeded with Aadhaar; payment in next cycle."

fields.description:
Date the remark was recorded. Absent until there is a remark. An IST calendar date; see CalendarDate.
Defined here because a portal may publish it. A pack whose portal does not refuses the field outright with not/required rather than leaving it defined and permanently absent.

PM-KISAN note: read from OfficeReplyDate.
Canonical OAN type, optionally accompanied by Provider-defined JSON-LD types.

The PM-KISAN registration number the grievance is filed under. It is both the identity the portal authenticates on and the enrolment the complaint is against, because PM-KISAN has no separate reference for either -- the upstream takes one field, IdentityNo, and nothing else names a case. That is why it carries the same x-beckn-path as PMFBY's applicationNo: on support it is the orderId, the thing support is required against.
Named for the enrolment rather than for the applicant. An earlier draft called it applicantId, which claimed the field names a person and sat one letter from PMFBY's applicantPhone -- inviting a caller to read the two as the same role and put a phone number in orderId. It names neither a person nor a contact: it names the enrolment a complaint is filed against, which is what applicationNo names on PMFBY. The two ends match so the pair reads as one slot.
Aadhaar is deliberately not accepted. The portal takes a token derived from one through /GrievanceAadhaarToken and carries it in the same IdentityNo field, which would make this value sometimes a stable reference and sometimes an ephemeral secret. Registration numbers only keeps it one thing, and keeps the upstream Type field a constant.
Not writeOnly, and no-echo is deliberately absent: the value is returned in orderId, which is the provider's slot to fill. Sending back the caller's own registration number over the same signed exchange it arrived on discloses nothing. no-log and no-trace are the markings that matter here and they are unconditional.
The rule is only non-empty and alphanumeric. Eleven alphanumeric characters is the documented shape, but nothing upstream enforces it, and a length rule taken from a tool docstring would reject a valid grievance before the farmer's complaint reached the portal. ASCII-only is on purpose: the upstream accepts Devanagari and other native-script digits and forwards them unconverted.

Category of the grievance. Unlike PMFBY, the portal publishes a closed list of ten codes, so the pack enumerates them and an unknown code is refused at the network edge rather than upstream. The code goes to the portal verbatim.

fields.requirement: At least one of code or name
